newsitem.title: HONG KONG: FEATURE-HK handover a prime profit opportunity.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-HK handover a prime profit opportunity.

text.p: Hong Kong's impending return to China has given merchants a chance to benefit from a transfer of another kind -- cash from tourists' pockets into theirs.
Hong Kong, a world leader of the quick-buck doctrine, is ready to swoop, from five-star hotels to guesthouses to parking garages, to extract the maximum possible from tens of thousands of visitors.

Travellers coming for the handover are paying full price and higher for hotel rooms in one of the world's most expensive cities. Many were asked to commit to stay longer than usual and pay full-price airline tickets well in advance.

Businesses have been vigorously testing what the market will bear. For example, boat rental prices for a one-day trip have more than doubled to HK$15,000 (US$1,900) for a junk with a 20-person capacity.

A lot is at stake for the tourism trade as Britain hands Hong Kong back to China on June 30 after 156 years of colonial rule. Tourists are forecast to spend HK$9.2 billion (US$1.2 billion) in June, a 35 percent rise over June 1996.
Hong Kong's second biggest earner of foreign currency, the tourism industry, may make a killing on the handover surge.
But below-normal bookings for after the handover have alarmed some industry experts and generated complaints that "bad publicity" was scaring away visitors to Hong Kong under China's control.
Ranjit Feth was one of those deterred, not by alarming headlines, but by a stiff hike in the price of his guest room just before the handover.
LAWMAKER SAYS HOTELS HAVE BECOME "GREEDY"

Renting a room while he looked for a finance job in Hong Kong, Feth was told the cost was jumping to HK$800 from HK$400 a night for the two weeks around the handover. "The owner told me, 'Everyone is increasing their rates,' " he said.
Feth returned to his home in Jakarta and will resume his job search when the rate drops back after the handover. "I thought the rate would go up, but I didn't imagine it would double," he said.
However, Feth is not resentful. "I am a pure capitalist," he said. "If that's the way it works, I will not complain."

Hotels had demanded full payments three months before the handover for room reservations. The hotels had long thought they would be fully booked for the handover period, but by May, the Hong Kong Hotels Association said there were plenty of rooms available.
Hong Kong legislator Howard Young said the hotels had become "greedy".

Jonathan Wall, editor of Business Traveller Asia Pacific magazine, said, "I think the hotels were expecting an enormous bonanza, and it didn't happen over and above the number of people who normally come at this time of year."
HIGH PRICE, FIXED-STAY DETERS JAPANESE
Hotels charged full price, which effectively meant an increase of 20 to 25 percent, and also imposed minimum length of stays, usually five days.
"I think the Japanese tourists were hit hardest. They don't usually stay that long when they visit Hong Kong," said one Japanese visitor.
James Lu, executive director of the Hong Kong Hotels Association, acknowledged that the five-night packages were not selling well. "A lot of the hotels are relaxing their requirements," he said.
The Hong Kong Tourist Association has advised member businesses against short-sighted moves to gouge the public.
"Hong Kong has a good reputation of value for money, and we want to maintain it," said Peter Randall, HKTA public relations manager.

News organisations, sending 4,000 journalists to cover the event, have also encountered high prices. One broadcast producer, who asked not to be identified, told of reserving a parking space near the site of the ceremonies.
"The price started out at HK$240 for a night, and kept going up to HK$3,000," said the producer.

Broadcasters also were being charged by hotels for prime camera sites on rooftops overlooking Hong Kong harbour. And the telephone company was accused of levying stiff minimum charges for telephone and broadcast lines.
Meanwhile, if any visitors have money left over, they can spend it on handover-related souvenirs, which some might call novelties but others rip-offs.

There are cans of "Colonial Air" advertised as "100 percent pure pomposity" selling at HK$55 (US$7) and a Barbie Doll dressed as a Chinese empress at HK$357 (US$46). One can toast the handover by drinking Chateau Hong Kong Vintage 1997, a wine described as having a bouquet "full of English nuts with a faint hint of mandarin."
